canonical_answers: Use balanced stoichiometry; mass fraction requires the carbonate molar mass and sample mass.

payload.text: A 2.50 g carbonate sample reacts completely and produces 0.0118 mol CO₂.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine the carbonate mass fraction and justify the mole relationship.

criteria.description: Use balanced stoichiometry; mass fraction requires the carbonate molar mass and sample mass.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mole ratio from the balanced carbonate-acid reaction (conservation of mass) lets you convert moles of CO₂ to moles of carbonate, and state the assumption that the reaction went to completion.

criteria.description: The mole ratio from the balanced equation applies conservation of mass to convert CO2 moles to carbonate moles, assuming the reaction reached completion.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how you would experimentally verify the CO₂ yield, identifying the mass of CO2 evolved as the measured variable and the initial sample mass as the variable held constant.

criteria.description: A valid check measures the mass of CO2 evolved while holding the initial sample mass constant across trials.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State one systematic error (e.g., CO₂ escaping before capture) and predict whether it would make the calculated carbonate mass fraction too high or too low.

criteria.description: CO2 escaping before capture undercounts moles of gas produced, making the calculated carbonate mass fraction too low.
accepted_variants: Equivalent scientifically correct notation and reasoning earn credit.
